title: Hungarian authorities uncover $20m during probe of Orbán-era minister
description: Nearly $20m (£14.8m) in cash has been found hidden in farm buildings and buried in forests as part of an investigation into a former minister of Vikto
body: Nearly $20m (£14.8m) in cash has been found hidden in farm buildings and buried in forests as part of an investigation into a former minister of Viktor Orbán, authorities have said.Miklós Seszták, who served as minister of national development for four of the ex-prime minister's 16-year rule, is accused of accepting bribes as part of a scheme involving the state transport company. He has denied any wrongdoing.Hungary's new Prime Minister Péter Magyar unseated Orbán in a landslide election in April on the promise of launching a sweeping anti-corruption drive.On Friday, following the two-day search for the cash - found in secluded locations across the country - Magyar described it as the end of the "mafia".Investigators found wads of banknotes in safes, buried in woodlands and hidden in agricultural and residential buildings and warehouses, as part of the probe into Seszták, the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) said in a statement.The cash amounted to "5,071,632,000 forints, €2,658,350 and $1,257,100", it added, bringing the combined value to $19.5m. It has been deposited into the Hungarian State Treasury, the body said. The NVVH was established to investigate allegations of corruption during the Orbán rule, which Magyar has dubbed "Operation Purgatory".Magyar promised Hungarians "regime change" during the election earlier this year and has set about undoing many Orbán-era policies since entering office.Allegations of corruption and cronyism have long dogged Orbán, who during the course of his tenure turned Hungary into what the EU characterised as an "electoral autocracy".

schema.headline: Hungarian authorities uncover $20m during probe of Orbán-era minister

title: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from closing Washington DC golf course for renovation
description: A federal judge has temporarily blocked the US government's closure of a historic golf course and park in Washington DC. US District Judge Ana Reyes h
body: A federal judge has temporarily blocked the US government's closure of a historic golf course and park in Washington DC. US District Judge Ana Reyes has been overseeing a months-long challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links, which he said would be closed from 15 November for extensive renovations.Reyes has said Donald Trump cannot close the park or its golf course, but added that his administration was not required to actively manage either.Trump, an avid golfer, has said his plans to upgrade the 106-year-old course will create "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World". The BBC has contacted the White House for comment. Declaring the current course "Trash Island", he announced in October it would be renovated over 15 months to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments" - despite the ongoing litigation.In a 30-page decision issued on Saturday, Reyes said the Trump administration's justifications for the proposed course closures were pretextual, and that the government violated at least two federal laws "to meet an arbitrary deadline.""The Government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely," Reyes wrote.She said the closure "runs counter to the public interest in utilising national parkland", adding that the government had not "plausibly identified any harm it would suffer from a temporary restraining order that preserves the status quo pending further proceedings".Her order will last until the 28 November.The legal dispute dates back to February, when the DC Preservation League and others sued over redevelopment plans for the park.The historic course, which sits 2 miles (3km) south of the White House, is one of three public courses run by the National Park Service in the nation's capital.The legal fight then escalated in October, when the NPS began to cut down hundreds of trees without notifying Reyes until 15 hours before work was set to begin. After the trees were cut, Reyes ordered the Trump administration to stop tree removal until at least 26 October and give her three business days' notice about making any other permanent changes. Despite the work stoppage, Trump announced that the course would be closed for 15 months from 15 November to accommodate the renovations. He also shared a rendering of the course redesign."The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect. It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous, and disease-infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall," he said in a post to Truth Social.Reyes has since separately opened an inquiry into whether the justice department attorneys "have made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated ethical rules".That included whether giving late notice to the court about the renovation plans was "done in bad faith" and whether the attorneys failed to correct previously false statements or withheld information.She said she would carry out the inquiry with a special master, an independent third party.

schema.headline: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from closing Washington DC golf course for renovation

title: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
description: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.The histori
body: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.The historic meeting between the respective leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters."The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Russia has confirmed the meeting. China has yet to react. No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior US official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025."President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of South-east Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation that helped resolve the Cold War.The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement that included China, which has been building up its arsenal.Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could create major hurdles and take years.Xi separately hosted both Putin and Trump in Beijing just days apart earlier this year, while the US president welcomed his Chinese counterpart to Washington in September. Beijing has become a crucial trading partner for Moscow since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which has isolated Russia and left it subject to Western sanctions.But a controversial US deal to import Russian diesel and the suspension of sanctions targeting the biggest buyers of Moscow's oil and gas - including China - heightened European concern about the Trump administration's softening towards the Kremlin last month.Trump and Xi have meanwhile sought to project warmer ties at summits in Beijing and Washington this year - though little significant progress appeared to have been made on key issues such as trade, their race for AI dominance, and Taiwan. The war in Iran has also been a sticking point, with Beijing the largest buyer of Tehran's oil and its largest trade partner.Chinese state media reported on Friday that Xi would take part in "bilateral" talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit, citing a foreign ministry spokesman, but has not reported on the trilateral meeting.Earlier this month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media that there were "signals confirming readiness" for such talks at the summit.

schema.headline: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says

title: Copper wire upgrade caused nationwide flight chaos, US transport secretary says
description: A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations was caused by an issue following a copper wire upgrade, Transport Secretary
body: A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations was caused by an issue following a copper wire upgrade, Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said.Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem was caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades, or faulty equipment.The US government does not believe it was as a result of a cyber-attack, although an investigation is still under way, Duffy said.Friday's suspension was the longest such incident since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US and the disruption is expected to last for days.Maintenance was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre by a contractor called L3Harris, a technology provider company, Duffy said.The US has "an incredibly old telecommunications system", he added."It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued," he said.The transport secretary explained that a router that was being worked on had started flooding other air traffic control systems and created communication issues with planes which led the government to shut down the airspace for safety reasons.Bryan Bedford, who heads the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), told the same news conference: "We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI related."On Saturday L3Harris said it had completed over 70% of the work to modernise communications infrastructure before the shutdown."We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop of our nation's air travel," it said in a statement."L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."No flights were allowed to take off from the continental US for more than four hours from 15:54 EST (19:54 GMT) on Friday.More than 3,500 flights were cancelled and more than 2,000 delayed in the US on Saturday, according to tracking website Flight Aware, as knock-on disruption continues.In some cases, passengers were left stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to the gates. Some international flights were allowed to depart US airports, in an apparent effort to clear space.Duffy warned that a similar issue could arise again unless the US Congress approved upgrades to air traffic control infrastructure.US President Donald Trump has requested $30.1bn for the upgrades. Both chambers of Congress are currently controlled by the Republican Party.Former TSA Administrator John Pistole told the BBC that "the fact that they were able to get it restarted in four-and-a-half hours is good news - it shows a resilience in the system - but what's to say it's not going to happen tomorrow?"A nationwide ground stop has only been ordered one other time since all flights were banned from take-off for several days following the 11 September 2001 attacks.

schema.headline: Copper wire upgrade caused nationwide flight chaos, US transport secretary says

title: Pope Leo speaks on community 'suffering' on visit to remote Andes
description: Cajamarca has lost the highest number of people to internal migration, with 729,000 people born there now living elsewhere in Peru.In his sermon, Pope
body: Cajamarca has lost the highest number of people to internal migration, with 729,000 people born there now living elsewhere in Peru.In his sermon, Pope Leo thanked those who had made the journey to him and emphasised the importance of never losing heart, despite life's difficulties.Santa Cruz is within the Diocese of Chiclayo, where Pope Leo served as bishop from 2015 to 2023. During his tenure, he visited Santa Cruz several times a year to minister to the town's rural population.On Saturday he returned by helicopter, where he was greeted by singing and cheering. He later did a tour in a popemobile, where he waved to people who had travelled from across the region to see him.Speaking at a local parish on Saturday, the Pope said he felt "joy" at being able to visit the small town once again."It is like a very big dream that the Lord has allowed this servant to come here," he said.Rev. Kevin Noriega, who was ordained in 2018 by the then-bishop, told Reuters the visit had brought "enormous hope and emotion" to Santa Cruz. He said: "People are eager to experience this Holy Mass ... because after so much time they will be able to see their bishop - 'Father Robert,' as they used to call him - now as the Holy Father."

schema.headline: Pope Leo speaks on community 'suffering' on visit to remote Andes

title: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
description: US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Presid
body: US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.The US has not confirmed Zelensky's comments, and a US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties".The Ukrainian leader's comments came after US envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky as part of US efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others while Russia has said another Nato member on its border is unacceptable.Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. It controls most of the industrial region of Donbas and Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine is unwilling to give up sovereign territory."The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.He went on to say that if he received a specific proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted. It has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.Other Nato members apart from the US are wary of membership for Ukraine - and it is understood that Ukraine itself sees that as unrealistic. The Kremlin has always been fiercely opposed, too. It is one reason why Russia started this war in the first place.It is possible the American envoys were exploring Ukraine's "red lines" when it comes to occupied land in the Donbas. Zelensky said recently that the US mediators believed Kyiv only had to cede territory to achieve peace and were applying pressure, keen to do a deal as soon as possible.Ukraine is sure that Russia's ambitions are far greater and has long seen Nato as its only sure protection.So it is also possible that Zelensky made this suggestion public in order to re-open a discussion that had been considered all but closed.He maintains that the idea is now "back on the agenda" as part of an "extremely difficult conversation" on European security.It also looks like Ukrainian push-back against Russia's renewed hardline stance. Moscow now talks about a "new European security architecture", which is long-standing Russian code for a weaker Nato.The issue appears to have been the main focus at the latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi this week.Hours after Zelensky's remarks, Jared Kushner appeared keen to dampen down any US offer of Nato membership for Ukraine, urging "confidentiality" in a sensitive process.He said that "maximalist" proposals had been reported from the negotiations, along with "strong political rhetoric".In what read like a reproach to Kyiv, Kushner referred to "private discussions" aimed at exploring new ideas about ending what he called a "horrible war".He said the hope was that those ideas might lead to new proposals or breakthroughs.Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas. It has insisted again that it will not agree to a ceasefire until a final peace deal is in place that would include Ukraine ceding control of those parts of the Donbas Russian troops have not captured, in addition to the Crimean peninsula Moscow annexed illegally in 2014.The latest round of talks come after a period of fraught relations between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities deep inside Russia, which Trump had asked Ukraine to pause to facilitate the supply of Russian diesel to ease global fuel prices.Zelensky then accused US officials of limiting Ukraine's Starlink internet service, which it uses to co-ordinate defensive operations, while Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" and called for fresh elections.Elections are suspended while Ukraine remains under martial law, but Zelensky has previously said he was willing to hold them within months of a peace deal being reached and would give up the presidency in exchange for Nato membership.

schema.headline: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says

title: Eurovision Asia: Philippines wins continent's first song contest
description: Figure caption, Philippines' Carmelle has won the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-SobraByJonathan HeadSou
body: Figure caption, Philippines' Carmelle has won the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-SobraByJonathan HeadSouth East Asia correspondent, in BangkokThuong LeReporting fromBangkok and Jack GreyBBC NewsThe Philippines have won the very first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, hosted in Bangkok and with 11 countries vying for the title.Nineteen-year-old singer Carmelle was always a front runner with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra, complete with its catchy rap section.She earned 211 points in total - 93 from the jury and 118 from the public vote - ahead of Thailand's MANG x DAOU in second place with 170 points.There was a joyous atmosphere at the One Bangkok Arena as the crowd cheered the contestants and celebrated the popular winner.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Carmelle was the youngest contestant in the competition at 19 years old Carmelle, the youngest contestant in the competition, was an obvious favourite with the juries and the public despite strong showings from several nations. Other notable acts included MANG x DAOU, whose emotive duet Aroma elicited huge cheers from the home crowd.Bangladeshi beatboxers Beatmosphere eschewed the traditional backing track, instead using their voices to replicate the sounds of drums and basslines.And Laos's Thinla performed her crowd-pleasing song Bae in a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit.However, the Laotian song had a unintentional second outing after the music video was played over an apparent technical issue during the broadcast - meaning it was the last song the audience heard before the vote. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Thinla wore a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit during her performanceThe voting system worked much the same as the European Eurovison, with the public vote accounting for 50% of the result and the other 50% coming from the 11 national juries - with additional points awarded from a rest of the world vote. Here's how the final scoreboard ended: 1. The Philippines - 211 points2. Thailand - 170 points3. Vietnam - 164 points4. Malaysia - 152 points5. Laos - 139 points6. Bhutan - 126 points7. Republic of Korea - 113 points8. Mongolia - 94 points9. Nepal - 69 points10. Cambodia - 61 points11. Bangladesh - 35 pointsAlso performing during the broadcast was 2026 Eurovision Song Contest winner Dara from Bulgaria, who performed her winning song Bangaranga and new song Bad Idea.Thai superstar Jeff Satur also made an appearance, hitting the high notes in his performance of Black Tie.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Vietnam's Toc Tien came third with 164 pointsEurovision in Asia was an idea that has been talked about for decades, but one that never seemed to materialise - despite many false starts - until now. There is a huge enthusiasm here for Eurovision Asia, but a large number of the audience were established fans of the original contest from other countries and regions of the world.Speaking after the show, fan Zelie Pereira - who travelled from Scotland to Thailand to attend - said she was "very happy" with Carmelle's win.Image source, BBC/Jack TranImage caption, Eurvosion superfans Michael, Scarlett and Zelie travelled from the UK to Thailand to watch Eurovision Asia's first outingKorea, Vietnam and Laos also received praise from Pereira and her friends Michael Peters and Scarlett Massie, both from England."It was amazing, a very high standard," said Massie."The dance was amazing. The sets were amazing. The costumes were amazing. The singing was amazing. Incredible", Peters added.They confidently declared that "Asia Vision" should be the name for next year's show.For some, it seems the excitement for another edition is already building.However the crowd at the One Bangkok Arena thinned out not long after the Philippines singer Carmelle lifted the trophy.The arena was crowded, but not full, and it's still not clear how much commitment there is among regional broadcasters to keep the contest going and expand it to more than 11 countries.

schema.headline: Eurovision Asia: Philippines wins continent's first song contest

title: Ebola in DR Congo: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola.
description: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can surviveImage source, Braton Serge/BBCByRuth AlongaBBC AfricaReporti
body: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can surviveImage source, Braton Serge/BBCByRuth AlongaBBC AfricaReporting fromButemboWhen Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified.They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there."Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him.But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive.This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded.Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience."As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works.The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate.Image source, Braton Serge/BBCImage caption, Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga uses his book to help convince sceptics that Ebola is realThe first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team.After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve.Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north.This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance.After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea.This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre."She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says.Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance.He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids.Image caption, Dr Kamwanga's mother says his experience has helped dispel some of the misinformation she had heard about EbolaThe current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment."The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea.In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding.Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified."I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains.Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok.The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him.However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged."We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC.For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region.He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance.Neighbour Kavugho Sifa shared these concerns."We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC.They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola. Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation.After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust."I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact." During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real.But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding.Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says."Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate".He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion.But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone.Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community.He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly."He agrees too with the recent report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) that Ebola funds are going missing."The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says.The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease."Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited."More from the BBC on the Ebola crisis:

schema.headline: Ebola in DR Congo: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola.

title: Judo champion Teddy Riner shakes up French presidential race with surprise candidacy
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Five-times Olympic champion Teddy Riner is one of France's most popular athletesByHugh SchofieldIn ParisApart from
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Five-times Olympic champion Teddy Riner is one of France's most popular athletesByHugh SchofieldIn ParisApart from an overwhelming urge to pin one's opponent to the floor of the house, there is no obvious connection between politics and the world of top-level judo.That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race.The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances.Riner is, after all, one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, regularly topping the polls for embodying the nation's "values". He is a proven winner, with five Olympic golds and 11 world championships under his belt, as well as a successful career in business.More than 28 million people have watched his election broadcast on Instagram and X, shot with proper presidential decorum against a backdrop of books and a French flag. Some 22% told an Ifop poll within 24 hours they "could" vote for him.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Teddy Riner's video has attracted 14.5 million views on Instagram aloneActors and television personalities have become presidents in other countries. The ex-leader of Liberia – George Weah – was formerly a professional footballer.So why not a judoka in the Élysée Palace?"Anyone who thinks that being out of the political in-crowd disqualifies Riner from running for the Élysée would be very wrong," says Guillaume Tabard of Le Figaro."But [Riner] too would be wrong if he thinks not belonging to the in-crowd is all it takes."For now the whole of the French political world has decided to take the Riner candidacy seriously – or at least to pretend to. That is partly because he is such a popular personality that mocking his political hopes could easily rebound badly.But it is also because the state of French politics – outside of the burgeoning forces of the hard left and hard right – is one of total disarray.The centre-ground is floundering, with no candidate yet emerging who can inspire anything like the sense of mission of hard-right leader Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the hard left, who for now look set to face off in the final round of the presidential election in May.So when a popular figure like Riner enters the race - proclaiming himself "neither left, nor right", wanting to "unite the country" and "put money back in people's pockets", railing equally against "racists" and "yobs who scare people off our streets" – politicians have to take note.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Hard-right leader Marine Le Pen currently leads the polls in the race to be France's next presidentIt is perfectly possible, probable even, that Riner's campaign will fizzle out after a brief period of hype, and that the judoka will after all be a joker in the pack. But it is also possible that it won't, in which case the pre-election arithmetic will need a hasty readjustment: and it won't be the centrists who are smiling.Thus far, Riner has shown himself a master of the codes required for this kind of out-of-nowhere candidacy, the first of which is to press home the message: "Don't Worry! I'm NOT a Politician!"In this day and age in France, anyone who smacks of the "system" is automatically downgraded in voters' eyes, so it is important to emphasise that you are only running for office because, one, you have experienced real life (unlike those loafers in Paris); and two, you have discovered that there are solutions out there for the country's many problems. Solutions that are invisible to those same blinkered apparatchiks.All this Riner was able to express in last Monday's social media broadcast by using sophisticated rhetorical devices."People say I am a fool for wanting to run for the presidency," he said."Am I a fool? Well, if refusing to see France sink under the weight of debt; refusing to see mothers and fathers grit their teeth every time they do their weekly shop, and tremble with fear when their kids go out on the street… if all that means being a fool, then yes call me a fool."It was a promising oratorial start for the sportsman, and certainly attracted the viewers. But if he is serious – and Riner says he never does anything half-heartedly - that's not how he became an Olympic champion – then the hard work begins now.What does Riner actually want to do? Who will be on his team? Where does he position himself on the all-consuming matters of the day: pension-reform,  investment in education, the cost of living, public debt, the rise of populism or Russia's war in Ukraine?In short, how does he intend to transform his undeniable popularity as a sporting figure into a political mandate?Image source, ReutersImage caption, Protesters have for weeks taken to the streets in France over wages, the cost of living and public services Broadly, Riner appears to be on the right on economic matters and law and order, but being black and of Caribbean background he is also very strong on racism. When he says he is anti-extremism, he is referring mainly to Marine Le Pen.In other words his pitch is somewhere in the centre, and against the extremes.The trouble is, this is already an extremely crowded area, with important figures like ex-prime ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal signally failing to take off.Currently there are a dozen or so candidates in the area between centre right and centre left, stretching from the Socialist-backed Raphaël Glucksman to the Republicans' Bruno Retailleau on the right.The latest possible addition is Christine Lagarde, who steps down as head of the European Central Bank next February.Image source, Pool/AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, President Emmanuel Macron is among the few politicians who appears genuinely pleased by Riner's decision to runThe addition of yet another contender will dilute their polling numbers even further, making a second-round qualification for Mélenchon more likely.So no wonder the leader of France Unbowed (LFI) seemed so happy about Riner's decision to run. "We know how it goes: neither right nor left means not left," Mélenchon told reporters on Friday.The only other politician who seems genuinely pleased, rather than putting on a fixed smile, is President Emmanuel Macron, who said Riner was a "great champion" and that politics "did not belong to the professionals".That could be explained by the president's cool relations with his former prime ministers, Philippe and Attal, both of whom are doing all they can to distance themselves from their unpopular one-time boss.Riner said he viewed Macron's praise as a "poisoned chalice", telling reporters on Saturday that he was "not the president's envoy, I'm not a Macronist".Politics and judo have very little in common, but of the two, as Riner will soon discover, the more vicious is not the one that is fought out hand-to-hand after mutual acknowledgement on the tatami mat. In Japanese, judo actually means "the gentle way".If he starts looking like a serious candidate, Riner must know his life will be turned upside down, not just his physical form. In politics you do not bow in respect to your opponent. You give him a metaphorical headbutt.

schema.headline: Judo champion Teddy Riner shakes up French presidential race with surprise candidacy

title: Muhoozi Kainerugaba: The general at the centre of Uganda's power struggle
description: In Uganda's military, even senior generals are finding that their rank offers little protection from the wrath of the country's powerful army chief.Ov
body: In Uganda's military, even senior generals are finding that their rank offers little protection from the wrath of the country's powerful army chief.Over the past 15 months, at least a dozen generals and senior officers have been arrested under Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the son of President Yoweri Museveni, in a crackdown that has unsettled the military's top ranks.The arrests come amid growing political tensions over who will succeed Museveni, who has ruled Uganda for four decades.Gen Kainerugaba, 52, is widely seen as a potential successor, although his ambitions appear to be facing resistance within the ruling party.This week, he threatened Vice-President Jessica Alupo with dismissal and possible arrest, while suggesting he should take her position.The ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) has, however, rejected reports that its senior leadership had rejected a proposal to back Gen Kainerugaba as the next president, describing the claims as "completely false".This has all fuelled speculation that the arrests are part of an effort to sideline military officers opposed to the general's presidential ambitions.Others see the arrests as evidence of an anti-corruption drive in which senior commanders are held to account.At the centre of the tension are two powerful powerful institutions: the military, where Gen Kainerugaba wields considerable influence, and the NRM, where questions about his political ambitions appear to be dividing senior figures.A recent meeting of NRM's top leadership ended without agreement on a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Museveni's successor, according to the AFP news agency. Five party sources who attended the closed-door meeting told AFP that a vote was abandoned after several members spoke against the proposal. Uganda's news website ChimpReports, however, said that most members who spoke backed the general's potential presidency, although some questioned his readiness for civilian leadership.In a statement on Thursday, NRM Secretary General Richard Todwong Awany confirmed that the party had met on 10 November to discuss "political, social and economic issues".He dismissed reports that the meeting had rejected a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Uganda's next president, saying the party would communicate any decisions "through the right channel, at the right time".Dr Gerald Bareebe, a Ugandan-born political scientist at Canada's York University, sees a connection between the arrests and political manoeuvring over Museveni's succession, often referred to as the "Muhoozi Project"."Senior officers believed not to support the project have been arrested, detained or charged with corruption and treason," he tells the BBC.He says the allegations against some officers were widely viewed as politically motivated, reflecting growing divisions within the military over the succession question.Some of those detained have since been released, apparently after securing the general's forgiveness.The detention of one of the country's most prominent former commanders, Lt Gen Peter Elwelu, has brought the crackdown into sharper focus.The former deputy army chief was detained on 2 November over allegations that he had plotted to destabilise the eastern Teso region.His fall from grace followed a series of social media posts by Kainerugaba, who accused him of treachery and announced that he had been stripped of his three-star rank and demoted."The traitor Peter Elwelu is hereby stripped of his ranks. He is demoted to Private," Kainerugaba wrote on X.He also claimed that more than 20 soldiers linked to Elwelu had been arrested.The announcement raised legal questions, with Ugandan media reporting that military regulations do not allow a senior officer to be stripped of his rank through a social media post.The army later confirmed Elwelu's detention, saying they had recovered 15 guns, military uniforms and two pickup trucks linked to him. His family has rejected the allegations.Elwelu is among at least a dozen generals and senior officers detained since April 2025, according to an investigation by Uganda's Daily Monitor newspaper.They include three former military intelligence chiefs who once oversaw some of Uganda's most sensitive security operations.Maj Gen James Birungi, a former head of defence intelligence and security, was arrested in August 2025, on allegations including treason, terrorism and corruption. He was charged before a military court but later released after Gen Kainerugaba announced that he had "forgiven" him.Another former intelligence chief, Maj Gen Abel Kandiho, was detained in September this year over allegations of providing false intelligence and treachery. He remains in detention, according to the Daily Monitor.His predecessor, Brig-Gen Charles Bakahumura, was also arrested in September over similar allegations, but was later released after the army chief announced that he had forgiven him.Other officers have faced accusations ranging from stealing military fuel to taking money to spy on military communications.The military has defended the arrests as part of efforts to tackle corruption and criminality within the armed forces.Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa says the arrests reflect investigations involving different security agencies, rather than an army-led purge.He argues that detaining senior officers helps protect witnesses and demonstrates the seriousness of the anti-corruption drive."Gen Muhoozi has the overall duty to permit the investigation team to arrest these high-profile people, in consultation with the commander-in-chief," Egesa says, adding: "The arrests are not summarily done."But Bareebe sees a wider political motive, arguing that officers suspected of opposing to Gen Kainerugaba's presidential ambitions are being targeted."The result is a broad purge that has affected both serving and retired officers perceived to be anti-Muhoozi," he says.He points to divisions between the elite Special Forces Command (SFC), which he says is largely loyal to the president's son, and army commanders who remain unconvinced about his succession.The allegations against the officers are at different stages, with some facing charges, others in detention without publicly announced charges, and several having been released.Bareebe also questions whether military trials can deliver independent proceedings."Many Ugandans regard the charges as politically motivated and therefore expect little justice," he adds.He alleges that some officers have had charges dropped after closed-door negotiations with the president and his son, during which they were pressured to declare support for Gen Kainerugaba.Government spokesperson Allan Kasujja dismissed the claims of a succession fallout as "hogwash".Unlike his predecessors, who communicated through official military channels, Gen Kainerugaba frequently uses X to announce arrests, criticise public officials and comment on domestic and international affairs. Some have sparked diplomatic controversy.On the night of 9 November, he turned his attention to Vice-President Jessica Alupo, demanding to take her job."Whoever is in that office should prepare to hand it over soon," he wrote, in posts that he later deleted. He also questioned Alupo's loyalty and threatened her dismissal, adding that the government would operate "on military terms", if he became his father's deputy.The following day, his X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, became inaccessible. It was unclear whether he deactivated it himself, which he has done before, or the platform had suspended it.Alupo remains in office and has yet to respond publicly. Egesa says Gen Kainerugaba's controversial posts reflect his preferred style of communicating, but adds that security analysts are assessing their implications for Uganda's political and military stability.Bareebe, however, sees them as part of a broader effort by the army chief to extend his influence into civilian politics.He says the public confrontation with senior political figures illustrates how the succession debate was spilling beyond the army and into the ruling party.Gen Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in March 2024, after previously commanding the SFC, which is responsible for protecting the president and strategic installations.Under Uganda's military structure, he reports directly to Museveni, giving him considerable influence over the army.Bareebe argues that the SFC's loyalty to the president and his son could prove crucial in any future transfer of power."The regular army remains important but has been sidelined by the SFC, which now functions as a personal army for Museveni and his son," he adds.At the heart of the tension is the question of who will succeed Museveni, 82, who has ruled Uganda since 1986, when his rebel National Resistance Army seized power after a five-year guerrilla war.He was sworn in for a seventh elected presidential term earlier this year, extending his rule into a fifth decade.Gen Kainerugaba has been regarded as a possible successor and has indicated that he intends to seek the presidency in 2031, when his father's current term is due to end.He also leads the Patriotic League of Uganda, a political movement that has mobilised support around his leadership.But recent developments suggest that a transfer of power from father to son may be more complicated than his supporters anticipated.At the recent meeting of the NRM leadership, one official reportedly urged Museveni to retire his son from the military and give him a civilian role to gain administrative experience, AFP reported.Local media reported that some party officials consider Gen Salim Saleh,  Museveni's younger brother, better suited for civilian leadership.There is, however, no indication that he is interested in becoming president.Others reportedly defended Gen Kainerugaba, pointing to his military leadership, anti-corruption campaign and grassroots political mobilisation.Bareebe says opposition to the proposed succession has grown within the NRM, with both veteran figures and younger members concerned about what they see as an attempt to secure power through coercion.He suggests Museveni's reluctance to move his son out of the military could reflect the importance of retaining control of the army during any transition."The underlying calculation appears to be that, so long as Muhoozi controls the SFC, he can use it to capture power even in an event of a contested transition," he says.The military has been central to Museveni's hold on power, making the loyalties of senior commanders particularly important as succession questions intensify.The family's military influence has also drawn attention to the possibility of a political dynasty spanning generations, with Gen Kainerugaba's son, Ruhamya, recently graduating from Britain's Sandhurst military academy.The succession debate is unfolding against a backdrop of sustained pressure on the opposition.Veteran opposition politician Kizza Besigye remains in detention on treason charges, which he denies.Bobi Wine, who came second to Museveni in this year's presidential election, has gone into exile in the US, after being threatened by Gen Kainerugaba.The government has consistently defended its security operations as lawful and necessary to maintain stability.For now, Museveni remains in power.But the arrests, his son's threats and competing accounts of divisions within the ruling party have intensified questions about how Uganda's next political transition might unfold, and what role his family may play.

title: CJP: India’s protesters face government crackdown after summer victory
description: After a summer win, India's Gen Z protesters face a winter of uncertaintyFigure caption, India's Gen Z protesters are facing the limits of dissentByAz
body: After a summer win, India's Gen Z protesters face a winter of uncertaintyFigure caption, India's Gen Z protesters are facing the limits of dissentByAzadeh MoshiriSouth Asia Correspondent, DelhiCheers erupted at Delhi's Jantar Mantar protest site in July as news broke that Gen-Z protests had forced federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign. One protester turned to me, beaming: "This is the youth's victory."Just over three months later, the mood has shifted dramatically. Student protesters are now struggling even to assemble. Demonstrations by the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) last month over voting rights were met with sweeping restrictions and thousands of peaceful protesters were detained.The summer had seen a new wave of dissent in India, driven by deep frustration among the youth and fuelled by irreverent online satire. The movement spread across the country, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a leader with a strongman image, unaccustomed to open criticism or mockery, struggled to contain it. But the government's increasingly forceful security response suggests it has learned from its rare concession to protesters, invoking public order to curb dissent.The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national spokesperson Syed Zafar Islam rejected accusations of heavy-handedness and told the BBC: "The right to protest and freedom of expression is mandated by the constitution, but it has to be done within the law. It cannot override the rights of others, at the cost of public security".This is by no means the first time the Modi government has faced large-scale protests. But the breadth of them pose a challenge for the BJP, according to Yamini Aiyar, former president of the Centre for Policy Research and visiting professor at Brown University.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The CJP led massive protests in July which ended with the resignation of a federal minister"They are not defined by caste, gender or economic class," Aiyar said. "Even some of the core BJP base, the upwardly mobile, lower-income classes, were attracted by the movement."The scale of the youth protests is also magnified by its online presence. Protesters have broken a longstanding political taboo, openly mocking the prime minister online."It's more than just laughs," said Sakhi, a student protester who identifies as they/them and affiliated with one of Delhi University's left-wing student organisations."The fear of repercussions in other generations isn't felt as much in ours," they said. "Comedy is a new language to challenge authority."Previous protest movements posed serious challenges to Modi but were easier to dismiss as representing narrow sections of society or to label "anti-national", according to Aiyar.In 2020, farmers protesting against controversial agricultural reforms were blocked from entering Delhi, leading to months of demonstrations and, at times, clashes on the capital's borders. After a year of protests, the government abandoned the reforms.Protests against a contentious citizenship law in 2019 and 2020 are a stark reminder of the powers of the judiciary should anyone be deemed a national security threat.Student activist Umar Khalid was arrested under anti-terror laws after violent clashes in Delhi that killed 53 people, mostly Muslims. He was accused of being a "key conspirator". He has now spent more than six years in jail without his trial having begun.His partner Banojyotsna Lahiri told the BBC they have no regrets, but that the situation instilled "a kind of fear that has prevailed".Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty ImagesImage caption, The CJP in its early days became a unifier for Indian youth frustrated with the state of education, jobs and economy "We are just looking at a very dark mesh of empty space, because we don't know when the endpoint is," Lahiri said. Khalid's latest appeal was lodged this month.Aiyar believes opponents are using a familiar "playbook" today to "de-legitimise" protests, but that it isn't resonating as convincingly.Nevertheless, the youth protests have struggled to recapture this summer's momentum.CJP leaders, including spokesperson Saurav Das, have faced repeated detentions and legal action. Das and fellow leader Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in Delhi's Tihar jail after being accused of trespassing at Jantar Mantar. The site of their summer victory has since been struck off the list of authorised protest venues, a decision being challenged in court.Protesters from other groups, including the left-wing All India Students' Association (Aisa), have also faced police action over allegations of defying orders."We were expecting some kind of crackdown," said Das. He added that "the government has learnt a lot" since the summer.Legal experts warn the proceedings themselves can have a chilling effect."A lot of cases can lead to acquittals, but it can take years. The process is the punishment, and that can deter protesters," said Ali Khan, an assistant professor at Lloyd Law College.The restrictions on demonstrations have become excessive, according to constitutional lawyer Vrinda Grover, who is advising the CJP.Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty ImageImage caption, Tens of thousands of people gathered at Delhi's iconic Ramlila Maidan for the opposition protest on 1 November"Those who are organising the protests have repeatedly emphasised that this is non-violent," she argued. "Rights have been whittled down in the name of law and order."The BJP has rejected suggestions it is suppressing peaceful dissent.Islam told the BBC that demonstrations "cannot override the rights of other citizens just because a handful of people want to protest and be responsible for violence".Even dissenting online carries risk. Sakhi's viral social media posts have attracted targeted abuse and transphobic attacks. The BBC has seen posts threatening them with violence and rape.Sometimes, it can deter Sakhi from protesting or even make them change the way they dress."Making people laugh can turn into being called anti-national," Sakhi said. "They want me to feel damaged," they added.They claim some of their content was removed after getting millions of views.Under India's information technology laws, the government can order platforms to block content on national security grounds. Notices on X and Instagram have shown accounts being withheld in India.CJP leaders have likened the crackdown to the 1975 Emergency, when then prime minister Indira Gandhi suspended civil liberties and jailed political opponents.Yet dissent has not been stamped out.Opposition parties have, in part, filled the void. Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi on 1 November for a rally organised by INDIA bloc, an alliance of opposition parties led by Congress, and permitted by the authorities.CJP leaders, meanwhile, insist the movement is bigger than their organisation.When Das walked out Delhi's Tihar prison on 21 October, photographs showed him smiling."I would just say wait and watch," Das told us. "Time is on our side. We are a very young generation."

title: What we know about the US ground stop and what to do if your flight is affected
description: On Friday afternoon, a government contractor called L3Harris was continuing work on upgrading an aviation telecoms network. As it swapped out copper l
body: On Friday afternoon, a government contractor called L3Harris was continuing work on upgrading an aviation telecoms network. As it swapped out copper lines for fibre at a remote location in the US, L3Harris installed a router - a piece of equipment which basically directs traffic across the network.According to Duffy, that router started flooding others in the air traffic control system, sending 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds.As a result, 17 out of 22 air route traffic control centres in the US experienced "instability" on voice and ground communications, said Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). It took the aviation authority 45 minutes to identify where the problem was because maintenance is logged manually on paper.This meant the FAA had to "pore through" the physical documents "to figure out who's working on what", Bedford admitted.As a precaution as it tried to track down the cause, Bedford said the decision was made to ground all flights.Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned".  He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."Duffy said the system needed a complete overhaul, estimating a $50bn price tag.In the meantime, he said authorities would work to determine whether it was "incompetence" or faulty equipment that led to the outage. He also said there would be "re-evaluation" of allowing upgrades to be done during the day. In a statement on Saturday afternoon, L3Harris confirmed it was working with the FAA to modernise the airspace communications infrastructure and said it was supporting the agency with its investigation. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," the firm said. Juliette Kayyem, US assistant secretary of Homeland Security under President Barack Obama, questioned why an upgrade was done on one of the week's busiest days for travel."You don't do it on a Friday when there's lots of air traffic controllers," she said"You try to find ways to minimise its upgrade so you're not maybe doing it across the board in a single moment but you also have to have systems that are ready to step in if the upgrade in any way begins to threaten the system," Kayyem added.A spokesperson for L3Harris said is it "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop of our nation's air travel".He added: "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."All US-bound air traffic from Eurocontrol member states was suspended.There are 42 Eurocontrol member states, including dozens of EU nations, the UK and Turkey, as well as Israel and Morocco.Passengers travelling from the UK have been warned of possible disruption on Saturday morning.A number of flights to the US from Heathrow airport were cancelled and delayed, but Manchester airport said no significant disruption was expected. Flights were operating as normal from Gatwick airport.Australia's largest international airport, Sydney, had grounded all US-bound flights, but scheduled flights are now expected to depart as planned.Air Canada also cancelled flights between the US and Canada.In the US, UK and the EU, airlines may be liable for compensation if the reason for a delay is deemed within their control, such as a fault with the plane or pilot sickness.As such, airlines do not have to provide compensation to passengers for air traffic control problems.But passengers are still protected to a certain degree under US federal - and country-specific - laws. Under the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, cancelled or "significantly delayed flights" - defined as three hours for domestic flights and six hours for international routes - must be offered alternative travel or a full refund of the fare if the passenger chooses not to fly. It also requires all air carriers to issue refunds for tickets purchased with credit cards within seven business days of the request, and 20 days for tickets purchased with another form of payment. Passengers accepting a new flight cannot receive a refund.In the US, there is no requirement for airlines to provide meal vouchers or accommodation, but some may offer complimentary support to customers. However, if passengers are travelling from the UK to the US or flying with a UK carrier, you may have additional rights. Under UK law, airlines have a duty to look after you when flights are delayed or cancelled for whatever reason.This includes:a reasonable amount of food and drink (often through vouchers)a way for you to communicate (often by refunding the cost of calls)free accommodation, if you have to stay overnight to fly the next daytransport to and from that accommodationIf your airline is unable to arrange assistance, you have the right to organise this yourself and claim back the cost later.The Civil Aviation Authority advises people to keep receipts and not spend more than necessary.It was only the second such nationwide stoppage since the immediate aftermath of the al-Qaeda plane hijackings of 11 September 2001."This looks like the worst since 9/11, but clearly not on that scale," Dr Guy Gratton, an associate professor of aviation at Cranfield University, told BBC Verify.Gratton pointed to a US grounding in 2023 due to a failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system."That lasted 1 hour and 52 minutes, delayed about 9,500 flights and cancelled about 1,300," he said.The 2023 outage meant air traffic safety notices could no longer be published and flights were grounded until that system was restored.

title: Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?
description: ByVictoria GillScience correspondentIn 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.Until that moment, the 11-year-
body: ByVictoria GillScience correspondentIn 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him.More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary – but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends.Jojo's carers at the Lekedi Foundation in Gabon want to find a companion - possibly another rescued or zoo-bred gorilla – that Jojo could live and bond with. But finding him a friend - and bringing them into his life - is not straightforward."He's probably the most extreme case of isolation I've ever seen in a great ape," says Prof Gillian Forrester from the University of Sussex, who is studying Jojo as part of research into great ape psychology and how to help rescued animals recover from trauma.Figure caption, Jojo's keeper Maxe Anaclet Makaba: 'He definitely feels lonely - you can see it in his eyes'Jojo was less than a year old – an infant clinging to his mother – when he was captured and sold.Most gorillas spend the first 14 to 19 years of their life in an embedded family unit but he was kept completely alone and on public display at the private zoo that bought him.Maxe Anaclet Makaba, who is head keeper at Lekedi and sees Jojo nearly every day, says it is clear he "craves human interaction"."He will even go to the trouble of gathering leaves for us to hold, so that we [trade them] for a treat – to interact with us," he says.Jojo also calls out when women he knows well visit his enclosure and then leave, making sounds that silverback males use to summon the females in the wild, explains Éric Willaume, who runs the sanctuary."He definitely feels lonely," he says.Image caption, When Jojo first arrived at the sanctuary after spending years in a small iron cage, he didn't look directly at peopleJojo is one of the more than 6,000 African primates estimated to have been bought or sold in the global trade of apes and other primates between 2000 and 2023. Thousands more are trafficked illegally for use as exotic pets, wild meat, and traditional medicine, the Pan African Sanctuary Alliance says., externalExperts believe when baby great apes are taken from their group at a young age like Jojo, they are left traumatised."If they're old enough to understand what happened to them, to understand their family was killed, they just lose the will to live," explains conservationist Tony King, from UK charity the Aspinall Foundation. "You see it in their eyes – the light goes out. I never knew where that expression came from, but I've seen it in gorillas."King – who specialises in rehabilitating rescued great apes – remembers rescuing two infant sister gorillas who were brought to a sanctuary in the Congo Basin. "They were clinging to each other," he says. "They stayed together in a little tight ball for about three days before they sort of unravelled. I think that's what kept them alive."Image source, Sinead Lynch/The Aspinall FoundationImage caption, Sisters Likendze and Matoko clutch each other after they were brought in a wooden crate to the Project Protection des Gorilles sanctuary in the CongoAfrican charity the Gorilla Rehabilitation and Conservation Education (Grace) Center uses what it calls "gorilla-led" rehabilitation. When the team rescues a young gorilla from the pet trade, they put it with a group as soon as possible so they can socialise and essentially learn to be a gorilla.But Jojo's case is unusual. He is fully mature and showing signs of harmful, chronic stress, according to Forrester.In a game-changing approach to studying anxiety and trauma in apes, she has used a thermal camera to film Jojo's face. This allows her to monitor blood flow, revealing what appears to be a chronically cold nose.It's a sign of a malfunctioning stress response. When any primate – a human, chimp or gorilla - is stressed, blood flow to the eyes and ears increases. It puts them on high alert for danger, but leaves their nose, temporarily, colder. For Jojo, this "nasal dip" as it is known, does not seem to recover."Being connected to others is incredibly important to our psychology as great apes," Forrester says. "Having another individual to share his life with would be so healing for him."I would assume other gorillas would help him process this grief and trauma."Image source, G ForresterImage caption, Thermal imaging of Jojo's face reveals signs of chronic stress, with a persistently cold nose indicating a potentially disrupted stress responseDr Katie Fawcett, from the Grace Center, says it's also "essential" for an animal to form social relationships to be considered for release into the wild - which is the ultimate goal for Jojo's keepers.The bonds between gorillas – what we would call friendship - is key to their society, adds Dr Robin Morrison from the University of Zurich, who studies the social lives of mountain gorillas. In one recent study, she discovered that female mountain gorillas would seek out females they knew, even if they hadn't seen them for many years, when joining a group.And she says a big part of a gorilla's normal social life is "just sitting together quietly sharing space".But Jojo has never been given the opportunity to sit quietly with another gorilla.No one knows how Jojo will react to a companion. Moving an animal from an accredited zoo would be a decision for an international committee and based on genetics, health and the animals' personalities and compatibility.Any introduction to another animal would be done very carefully – perhaps giving them an object that smells of the other before they see each other. These slow, cautious ape introductions do happen – when an animal moves from one zoo group to another, for example. Forrester has contacted a number of accredited zoos to explore the possibility of doing this for Jojo. But those discussions have fizzled out with no sign of progress.The problem, she says, is "there aren't clear processes in place to do these kinds of trans-locations".Image source, Dian Fossey Gorilla FundImage caption, Encounters between two or more separate gorilla groups are complex social eventsThe international rules and processes for moving captive gorillas across international borders - from one zoo or safari park to another - are designed for breeding programmes."They're not designed for reintroductions into the wild, or to find companions for animals that might need them," says Forrester.And because Jojo, who is probably in his 20s, has reached maturity, King thinks it might be too late for him to bond with other gorillas."Jojo's situation is unique, but he is probably best where he is," King says, adding that introducing him to another animal could, somewhat ironically, be a source of more stress for him.Image source, G ForresterImage caption, Prof Forrester studies Jojo as part of research to understand how our understanding of human mental health - particularly stress and trauma - can be applied to our great ape relativesBeing alone is also natural, even relatively common, for mature male gorillas. According to Morrison, about a third of adult males are solitary. "When they reach adolescence, they tend to disperse and spend a good chunk of their life on their own."Solo males will try to persuade females to form a group with them, but some don't succeed and may feel lonely as a consequence, Morrison believes. "If we think of loneliness in an evolutionary context - this mismatch between the social interactions they want and the social interactions they're getting. I suspect feeling lonely is part of the natural, evolutionary drive to attract females."But while those phases – of family life and adult solitude - play a role in wild gorilla society, Jojo was forced into solitary confinement as an infant.Morrison believes Jojo is probably both traumatised and lonely."[In the wild] gorillas move together, find food together, sleep together," she says. "So much of their lives is just being with this group."That is what Jojo's keepers, Forrester, and others want for Jojo. A friend. Maybe a female, or a compatible male."It would be good for him to have a companion," says keeper Makaba. "Because being alone is like being cut off from the world - it's like being in prison. "Having another gorilla there would be a good thing for him."GorillasGabonEnvironmentPrimates

schema.headline: Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?

title: Watch: Inside Ukraine power plant under constant drone threat
description: As peace talks between Ukraine and Russia continue, Ukrainians are facing a rolling schedule of planned power cuts because of intensified Russian atta
body: As peace talks between Ukraine and Russia continue, Ukrainians are facing a rolling schedule of planned power cuts because of intensified Russian attacks on their energy grid. Ukraine has responded by striking Russian oil refineries.Officials are concerned that life will quickly become unsustainable for millions of Ukrainians if power supplies cannot be maintained for at least four hours per day. Some privately warn that's close already, as some families are living with outages of up to 20 hours in Kyiv.Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson visits one of the country's power stations on the front lines of the war. Devastated by a direct ballistic missile strike, repair work is hampered by frequent air raids. Read the BBC's dispatch from Ukraine.

body: SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket on its return to Earth for the first time."Can you believe it?," a commentator said as large crowds cheered at the launch site in Texas.The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday. The booster was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea.The top part, known as the Ship, returned to Earth a few minutes behind schedule at around 15:20 local time (21:20 GMT) on Saturday, in the first-ever successful catch attempt.Read more on this story: SpaceX successfully catches top of huge Starship rocket for first time
